title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 261
paragraphs: The reason why those Egyptians I have mentioned do not sacrifice goats, female or male, is this. The Mendesians count Pan among the eight gods (and these eight gods, they say, came into being before the twelve gods), and the painters and image-makers represent the figure of Pan in painting and sculpture just as the Hellenes do — with goat's face and legs, not supposing him really to be like this, but making him resemble the other gods. The reason why they represent him in this form I prefer not to say. The Mendesians, then, reverence all goats, and the males more than the females (and goatherds too have greater honour than other herdsmen); but one of the goats in particular is reverenced, and when he dies there is great mourning in all the Mendesian district. Both the goat and Pan are called in the Egyptian tongue Mendes. Moreover, in my own lifetime there occurred in that district this marvel: that is to say, a he-goat had intercourse with a woman publicly, and this was done so that all men might have evidence of it.
